USMLE-style practice · Pharmacology

Electric-shock facial pain

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A 59-year-old man has recurrent seconds-long bursts of unilateral electric-shock pain in the cheek, triggered by shaving and chewing. Neurologic examination is otherwise normal. Carbamazepine is prescribed. Which condition explains this use outside epilepsy?

  1. Bell palsy
  2. Temporal arteritis
  3. Myasthenia gravis
  4. Parkinson disease
  5. Trigeminal neuralgia
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Trigeminal neuralgia

Brief triggered paroxysms in a trigeminal distribution are characteristic of trigeminal neuralgia.

Understanding the options

Trigeminal neuralgia
Brief triggered paroxysms in a trigeminal distribution are characteristic of trigeminal neuralgia.
Bell palsy
Bell palsy causes facial weakness rather than triggered shock-like pain.
Temporal arteritis
This usually causes persistent headache and ischemic symptoms rather than this stereotyped pattern.
Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness, not electric-shock pain.
Parkinson disease
The hallmark is a movement disorder, not paroxysmal facial pain.
